findings: Concurrent requests already using the current token race against a parallel refresh: refreshToken() invalidates oldToken server-side 'the moment it receives the request', but since every call site invokes getToken() independently with no shared request queue, any request already in flight (or dispatched moments later) with that same token gets rejected once the refresh lands — this is the direct mechanism behind the reported intermittent logouts.

refreshToken() is called with no try/catch/finally: if it throws (network failure, or a 401 because oldToken was already invalidated by a competing refresh), 'refreshing' is never reset to false and 'currentToken' is never updated. Every subsequent getToken() call then permanently falls into the wait branch, so one transient failure wedges the client into indefinitely returning a stale/expired token until a full page reload.

The 'wait' branch synchronizes via a boolean flag plus a single fixed 50ms sleep rather than awaiting the actual in-flight refresh's result/promise. If the refresh takes longer than 50ms (routine on a slow network), the waiting caller unconditionally returns whatever is currently in 'currentToken' — still expired — with no re-check loop and no re-validation of expiry.

On the very first getToken() call of a session, if two calls arrive concurrently before any token has ever been fetched, the second caller finds 'refreshing' already true, sleeps 50ms, and returns 'currentToken' — which can still be null if the first refresh hasn't completed in that window — handing the caller a null token instead of a valid one.
